title: Becoming a teacher
hookLine: the Buddha sends his monks out to wander, and a stranger learns from the way one of them walks

cards: A monk named Assaji is walking through the city of Rajagaha on his alms round, bowl in hand. He isn't preaching. He isn't saying anything at all.
A young wanderer named Sariputta, a pupil of another teacher who is still searching for the deathless, sees him and stops.

Something in the way this monk moves, going forward, looking back, eyes down, calm, makes Sariputta follow him down the street. When the round is done, he asks: who is your teacher, and what does he teach?
Assaji says he's new, and can only say a little. A little turns out to be enough.

teach.h: GO AND WANDER, FOR THE GOOD OF THE MANY.
teach.b: That scene comes from the Vinaya, the book of the monastic discipline.
A little earlier in the same book, the Buddha has a small group of monks who have understood the teaching, sixty, the text says, and he sends them out.
Go and wander, he tells them, for the good of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world. And don't let two of you take the same road.
So teaching begins as walking: roads, villages, alms rounds, not lecture halls. And the Assaji story shows what that can look like: a person whose way of moving made someone else curious.
The lesson started before a word was spoken. The Dhammapada puts the order plainly.
In Max Muller's translation: "Let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others; thus a wise man will not suffer."

Yourself first, then others; the verse doesn't let the second step come before the first. This week looked at teachers near and far, well-known and forgotten. Today the arrow turns toward the listener.
In this picture, nobody needs a title to teach. Someone who practices is often being watched by someone else: a child, a roommate, a coworker who notices how they handle a bad morning.
Becoming a teacher, here, is less a decision than something that happens when practice shows.

how: In Buddhist communities, monastics are expected to teach through conduct as well as words, and many lay Buddhists speak of practice at home and work as the way they pass the teaching on.

games.q: you're Assaji. a stranger stops you after your alms round and asks who your teacher is and what he teaches. you're new. what do you do?
o: say you're not qualified and walk on.
say you're new and can only say a little, then say it.
give a long sermon to impress him.
games.why: Assaji admits he's new and gives a short answer. it's enough for Sariputta, who goes on to become a great disciple.

practice: Let the body settle, upright and easy, the way Assaji might have walked: not stiff, not showing off.

Bring to mind one person who will see you today, and pick one small thing you'd want them to catch from you without being told: patience in a line, putting the phone down when they talk, a real thank-you.
Don't plan a speech; just let that one thing be the lesson.

wordCard.voice: Carika. The wandering the Buddha sent his monks on, so that the way they moved taught before they spoke.

orig.note: Pali carika: a wandering, a journey on foot; the word the Buddha uses when he sends the monks out.

carryVoice: Your line: by example. Yourself first, then others, as the verse says. Go gently.
